extracted.intended_audience: students and lovers of English poetry; aspiring poets and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical guidance for judging and composing poetry, with illustrated standards drawn from Homer, the Bible, Dante, Ossian, Chaucer, and other exemplars. Emphasises what makes verse 'poetry' (imaginative force, form, subject-matter, diction, and feeling) and warns against common defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry ≠ mere verse; content not form alone
rubrics_metrics.description: All is not poetry that passes for such: nor does verse make the whole difference between poetry and prose. The Iliad remains poetry even in a literal translation, while some rhymed pieces (e.g., Addison's Campaign) are only a 'Gazette in rhyme.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate beyond surface features (rhyme, metre): ask whether the work possesses the imaginative power and qualities of poetry rather than merely poetic dress. Examples: literal translations of Homer preserve poetry; some rhymed pieces do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry should 'lift the spirit' and strike the imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: That which lifts the spirit above the earth, which draws the soul out of itself with indescribable longings, is poetry in kind — poetry strikes and fixes the imagination, makes the eye of childhood glisten, and is not afterward thought of with indifference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the piece provokes involuntary, lasting imaginative response or exaltation. Works mixing fancy and reality (Pilgrim's Progress, Robinson Crusoe, Boccaccio) may attain this quality even if not strictly 'poetry' by form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneity and voluntary sympathy (avoid forced effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry produces instantaneous sympathy; the sympathy excited must be a voluntary contribution, not a tax imposed by incessant labour or mechanical contrivance. Forced, overworked interest (as in Richardson's romances) lacks elasticity and motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for over-manipulation: repetition, contrived artifices, 'infinite number of little things' that demand attention but do not let feeling arise naturally are anti-patterns. Prefer work where fancy runs ahead of the writer rather than being 'dragged along with an infinite number of pins and wheels.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is the eloquence of the imagination; avoid disputable/didactic subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between poetry and eloquence is that the one is the eloquence of the imagination, the other of the understanding: eloquence tries to persuade the will and convince the reason; poetry produces its effect by instantaneous sympathy. 'Nothing is a subject for poetry that admits of a dispute.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer subjects that invite imaginative, sympathetic response rather than argumentative debate or didactic demonstration. Didactic, disputable topics are better handled as prose or oratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere poetic diction and studied ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Some admired pieces are only 'poetry in the rhyme' and in the studied use of poetic diction; French poetry often 'wants the forms of the imagination' and is didactic rather than dramatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate diction for authenticity and imaginative necessity rather than for artificial ornament. If elevated language or stock poetic commonplaces are merely decorative without imaginative force, they are a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homeric standard: principle of action and heroic magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer's poetry is heroic: the principle of action or life is predominant; it is full of life and action, bright as day, strong as a river. His poetry is 'the poetry of number and form' — multitudinous, splendid, true, varied, and concerned with bodies as well as souls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging epic or narrative poetry, assess vitality, kinetic energy, largeness of scale, vivid crowd-scenes, formal rhythm ('number and form'), and truthful physical description as marks of Homeric excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biblical poetry: imagination and faith; immensity over multitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetry of the Bible is that of imagination and of faith: abstract, disembodied, not of form but of power; it aggrandizes into one (immensity), deals with solitude and original forms of nature, and often arises from a sense of Providence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for grandeur of vision, metaphors of boldness, concentrated massing of ideas, and a tone of faith or prophetic seriousness rather than decorative multiplicity. Biblical poetry's power lies in immensity, not in profuse detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dante's model: intensity, inward passion, and imaginative fusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Dante personifies blind will: his genius is a sullen heat, power, and passion. He combines internal feelings with external objects, lending his mind's power to the objects rather than borrowing from them; his earnestness sustains interest even amid improbability, and he leaves room to the reader's imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value intensity of vision, moral or emotional seriousness, a fusion of subjective feeling with external imagery, and an author's sustained earnestness. Expect possible obscurity or abruptness but judge by the sustained imaginative force and ability to make objects potent through character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ossianic quality: mastery of mood—privations, loss, and desolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ossian's poetry conveys the sense of privation and loss of all things (friends, country, good name); it is the poetry of decay and old age, conversing with departed spirits, with cold moonlight and barren imagery producing a perfect feeling of cheerless desolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For elegiac or nostalgic poems, assess how fully and authentically they evoke mood, loss, and haunting remembrances. The power lies in consistent tonal control and concentrated atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chaucerian standard: truth of nature, realism, and typifying character-drawing
rubrics_metrics.description: Chaucer is practical: his poetry reads like history, giving literal, discriminating description; similes and metaphors are few and 'for use' not ornament. He dwells on the essential, is scrupulous about the literal preference, and paints characters as samples of a kind (types) so that costume and external detail 'speak for themselves.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate character portrayal by verisimilitude, aptness of external detail as sign of inner life, economy of material (parsimony), and tactile/sensory exactness. Praise simple, direct depiction that seems like eyewitness description rather than mannered display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and tactile description: 'effect of sculpture' on the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Good description has tangible character — words point like an index; descriptions give the feeling of air, coolness, moisture, and local truth (gusto). There is strength as well as simplicity when imagination reposes entirely on nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess imagery for sensory concreteness and sculptural solidity. Avoid affected rapture; prefer descriptions that arise from inward delight in nature and convey a convincing sensory presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend of the picturesque and the dramatic
rubrics_metrics.description: In Chaucer the picturesque and the dramatic are closely blended: external appearances indicate character, and inanimate objects reflect or return the speaker's sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge scenes by how well setting and objects are integrated with character and emotion—do landscape and props enhance the dramatic effect rather than serve as mere decoration?
